title: Giant Beetle Larvae Are Quietly Eating Blueberry Roots
summary:
North Carolina's blueberry growers are facing a new threat from a destructive beetle whose larvae feed underground, damaging plant roots and potentially killing blueberry bushes. Scientists have now identified the insect responsible, an important first step toward protecting crops from the pest.

A research team at North Carolina State University has confirmed that the culprit is Prionus imbricornus, a species of longhorn beetle distinguished by its long antennae. These wood-boring insects are becoming a growing concern for blueberry producers in the state.

Female beetles generally lay their eggs in soil near the roots of hardwood trees. After hatching, the larvae feed on the roots, sometimes destroying enough tissue to kill the tree. The larvae can reach an impressive five inches in length, while the adult beetles do not feed at all.

North Carolina is the first state to document P. imbricornus feeding on blueberry bushes. But signs of a similar problem have existed for years. Reports of unidentified Prionus larvae damaging blueberry roots date back to 2010, but researchers had struggled to determine which species was responsible.

Part of the challenge was the insects' underground habitat. Because the larvae remain near plant roots, they are difficult to locate and study. Making matters more complicated, larvae from different longhorn beetle species often look remarkably similar, making visual identification unreliable.

According to Kenneth Geisert, a graduate student at NC State and lead author of the study, this uncertainty has made it difficult to develop pest control strategies. "Before now, researchers often just assumed the species of Prionus on their commodities based on adult identification," Geisert said. "If that guess was incorrect, it could mean using a treatment strategy that did not line up with the problem and incorrectly associating species and their hosts. For instance, while P. imbricornus attacks roots, another type of longhorn beetle might attack the trunk of a tree, or dead branches. Without knowing which species of beetle you're dealing with and their ecology, incorrect management can cause adverse effects on non-target insects."

To identify the insects, the research team did fieldwork at six blueberry farms in North Carolina's Pender, Sampson, Bladen, and New Hanover counties. The scientists installed black panel traps containing sex pheromones, chemical signals that attract adult beetles. After collecting the insects, they used a DNA identification technique known as genetic barcoding to determine the identity of larvae found in the fields.

This method examines short, standardized sections of DNA and compares them with reference sequences from known species. By matching genetic material from the unidentified larvae with DNA from adult Prionus beetles, the researchers could determine which species was present. The analysis produced a 98 to 99 percent match with P. imbricornus, confirming the identity of the beetle behind the root damage. Identifying the pest is an important breakthrough, and it is also the first step toward finding the right way to fight it.
why_it_matters: Knowing the exact pest lets farmers pick a treatment that works and avoids harming helpful insects, protecting a food crop and the farms that grow it.

background_read: Blueberry bushes are a crop, and like other crops they can be attacked by insect pests that eat their roots, stems, or fruit.
Longhorn beetles are a large family of insects named for their extra-long antennae, and many of them lay their eggs near trees so their larvae can feed on wood or roots underground.
Because the larvae live out of sight and look alike across species, scientists often need DNA tests to tell one kind from another before they can choose the right way to control it.
Knowing exactly which pest is present matters, because different beetles attack different parts of a plant and need different treatments.
Article_Structure: LEAD: North Carolina blueberry growers face a new pest: beetle larvae eating roots underground, and scientists have now named the culprit.
KEY EVENT: NC State researchers confirm the pest is the longhorn beetle Prionus imbricornus.
├─ WHO: A research team at North Carolina State University, led by graduate student Kenneth Geisert.
├─ WHAT: Larvae up to five inches long feed on blueberry roots and can kill bushes; adult beetles do not feed at all.
├─ WHEN: Mystery root damage reported since 2010; North Carolina is the first state to document this species on blueberries.
├─ HOW: Black panel traps with sex pheromones caught adult beetles, and genetic barcoding matched larvae DNA at 98 to 99 percent.
└─ WHERE: Six blueberry farms in Pender, Sampson, Bladen, and New Hanover counties, North Carolina.
EVIDENCE: The DNA match of 98 to 99 percent with P. imbricornus, plus traps that attracted adult beetles.
OPEN QUESTION: How to fight the pest now that it is identified — the right treatment still has to be found.

perspectives.description: Guessing the species from adult beetles can lead to the wrong treatment, which may fail against the real pest and harm insects that were never the target.
